1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6.background: Aron Nimzowitsch defended declining the gambit in My System, arguing that it loses no tempo because b4 does nothing for development anyway. Most commentators nevertheless judge declining weaker than accepting the pawn and returning it later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.strategy: Threatens a5, after which the bishop on b6 has no safe square: the a7 pawn blocks its retreat and the b4 pawn covers c5. Black must make room at once, and White keeps a lasting space advantage on the queenside.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.B.strategy: Brings the bishop to the long diagonal, so that e5 is attacked a second time and has only the knight to defend it. A natural, developing move, but it does not threaten the bishop on b6 the way a4 does.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.B.name: Italian Game: Evans Gambit Declined, Cordel Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.strategy: Chases the knight in the hope of winning e5, but the pawn has nowhere to go from here. The knight steps to a5 with tempo, hitting the bishop on c4, and White's attack turns out to be premature.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.a.strategy: Makes room for the bishop: without it, a5 would trap the piece on b6. The a-pawn move is the useful one here, keeping the bishop on its diagonal and the centre intact, and Black accepts a modest space deficit on the queenside.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 Bb6 5.b.strategy: Saves the knight and attacks the bishop on c4 in the same move. The cost is that e5 loses its defender, so White can win a pawn, but Black gets active play in return and White's king is still in the centre.
